maya: Heads-up — hitting flakiness in the python-async SDK around service-account impersonation + streaming reconnects.

maya: Flow: app creates impersonated creds to call other-project model endpoints. Using short-lived tokens (1m) and background refresh task that wakes every 30s. On a streaming socket reconnect we sometimes get 401s for ~10s before refresh picks up. Suspect two issues: refresh jitter + reuse of old token in in-flight requests.

maya: Minimal snippet:```python
# pseudo
creds = ImpersonatedCreds(target='projects/42', lifetime=60)
client = AsyncClient(auth=creds)
# background refresher
async def refresh_loop():
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(30)
        await creds.refresh_if_needed()
```

tom: @maya ok — couple quick things: 1) lifetime=60 is quite short for async background loops; any GC/stop-the-world pauses can push you past expiry. 2) how does refresh_if_needed determine "needed"? If it checks expiry < now + safety_window that's better than fixed sleep.

sasha: also check if the client caches an Authorization header per connection. If streaming reconnect reuses a cached header from an old connection object you can still send the stale token until the next handshake.

maya: refresh logic is naive: it just checks creds.expiry < time.time() then fetch. No pre-warm. Also the streaming lib holds headers in the connection and reconnect path re-attaches them without re-evaluating creds.

leo: Suggested tweaks I've used: 1) increase lifetime to 5m when possible; 2) implement proactive refresh: refresh if expiry < now + 45s; 3) on reconnect path always call auth.get_header() which forces a sync refresh check.

leo: pseudo fix:```python
async def maybe_refresh(creds):
    if creds.expiry - time.time() < 45:
        await creds.refresh()
# during reconnect
headers = await maybe_refresh_and_get_headers(creds)
```

maya: good call. One wrinkle: we need to impersonate across projects so we do a token exchange with target_audience (aud) to hit a model endpoint that expects a specific audience. Does that change pre-warm behavior? i.e., is aud-bound token non-reusable for other endpoints and thus more likely to expire/throw?

sasha: aud makes tokens specific but shouldn't affect timing. More important: if you generate token A for audience X and then later try to call audience Y you'll need a new token. Ensure your cache key includes (aud, scopes, subject).

tom: Also watch for clock skew. If VM time is off a few seconds you can see transient 401s. Add 5-10s leeway.

auth-bot: [system] detected 401 spike for maya-service between 2028-07-11T14:02:00Z and 2028-07-11T14:02:12Z (12 errors).

maya: nice catch @auth-bot — that's the window. We'll try proactive refresh + include aud in cache key. Quick question: best practice for jittering refreshes across many clients to avoid thundering herd?

leo: Add randomized jitter when choosing refresh thresholds and use per-process randomized offset. e.g., refresh_before = base - random.uniform(0, jitter). For central token brokers, exponential backoff and small randomized retry helps.

sasha: If you're running many workers in same pod, use a single shared token refresher rather than everyone hitting IAM at the same moment. Or use local advisory lock + leader election to have one refresher.

maya: ok doing these changes. I'll also add a reconnect hook to explicitly call get_auth_header() before starting stream.

tom: One more: when doing impersonation via IAM token exchange, ensure you request proper "delegates" chain; if you request on-demand short lifetime some providers return a token with a shorter-than-requested TTL. Log the returned expiry to be safe.

maya: great — logging expiry now. Thanks all :thumbsup: Will follow up if it persists and paste logs.

sasha: if you want I can sketch a small helper for python async client that wraps refresh + header retrieval.

maya: would love that. thanks!
